author: Slidebean
description:
Threads just quietly became bigger than X.

According to new data reported by TechCrunch, Meta’s Threads now has more daily active users than X, and it happened way faster than almost anyone expected.

The app launched just 18 months ago, and it already surpassed what used to be Twitter. And the reason isn’t some viral moment or a killer feature.

It’s distribution.

Every time you open Instagram or Facebook, Threads is right there. You’re not being asked to download something new, you’re just nudged to tap once. Meta turned its existing ecosystem into a launchpad.

While X struggled through controversy after controversy, Threads just kept shipping. Search, trending topics, web access, hashtags, feature by feature, month after month, quietly closing the gap.

But the real story isn’t Threads versus X.

It’s infrastructure versus independence.

Meta doesn’t need Threads to win on its own. It just needs it to be the default option inside apps billions of people already use every day.

title: Threads just passed X and the reason matters for founders.

author: Slidebean
description:
When startup speed meets human stakes.

Bionics AI won TechCrunch Disrupt in 2023.
By January 2025, it was FDA cleared for prenatal diagnostic support.

That pace would be impressive in SaaS. In medicine, it raises harder questions.

This AI helps detect abnormalities in unborn babies, insights that can influence life changing medical decisions.

Innovation is accelerating faster than our comfort with it. And stories like this force us to ask: when does “move fast” stop being a virtue?

title: This startup went from pitch competition to diagnosing unborn babies in two years

ShotSpotter promised to use AI to detect gunfire, dispatch police faster, and make cities safer.
Instead, it quietly put millions of Americans under constant audio surveillance, triggered thousands of false alarms, and became one of the most controversial government tech contractors in the country.

In this video, we travel to Chicago — one of ShotSpotter’s biggest customers — to investigate how the system actually works, why so many alerts never lead to real crimes, and how internal reclassification of audio turned a safety product into a legal and ethical nightmare.

This is the story of how flawed data, lobbying, and surveillance tech collided — and why once a city buys into systems like this, it’s almost impossible to walk away.
